newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile's Escondida operating at 85 pct normal - CEO.
newsitem.headline: Chile's Escondida operating at 85 pct normal - CEO.

text.p: A strike by 350 people at Chile's giant Escondida mine has slowed down operations slightly but output of both concentrates and cathodes is normal, the mine's CEO Ken Pickering said.
Pickering, speaking through a spokeswoman, said the mine was operating at 85 percent of normal levels and that the mine was redistributing work crews to ease the effects of the three-day-old walkout.
"Production of concentrates and cathodes is at full, normal levels. Ore supply from the mine is fully normal," said Pickering.

"With reduction of 350 people, our ability of total mine movement, that is ore and waste, is affected slightly but we are operating at 85 percent of normal levels after three days of strike," said Pickering.
"This total production in the mine is expected to improve as the manning of the mine operation crews is redistributed. The ore exposure situation within the mine is good," he added.
Pickering, visiting Escondida's offices in the northern city of Antofagasta, gave no direct answer to questions about reports that the concentrator was operating with limited stockpiled ore.
The spokeswoman relayed his comments verbatim to Reuters.
Owned by Australia's Broken Hill Proprietary and RTZ Corp plc of Britain, Escondida employs about 2,000 people at the open pit mine, concentrator and port at Puerto Coloso near Antofagasta.
The mine's unionized work force, about 350 people, began an indefinite strike last Friday to press for progress in wage negotiations.
Though involving relatively few people, the strike is being closely watched in Chile's booming private copper mining industry.

The union's goal is to win a contract better than the individual contracts signed by the non-unionized workers. The non-unionized workers will then have the option of taking the union contract, thus potentially enlarging the union rolls and giving Chile's mineworkers' unions a big victory in efforts to organize Chile's new crop of huge private mines.
A spokesman for the Escondida miners' union said contacts with management were not prospering.
"The company has not even received the union leadership. There has been no positive proposal to the workers," said the spokesman in Antofagasta.
Union leaders were due to meet with workers Monday night to decide on the next steps to take, he said.
Mines at state-owned Codelco are already completely unionized and are the scene of agonizing negotiations whenever contracts come up from renewal.
